implementation_notes: Ruby's core library provides the queue: Thread::Queue is a multi-producer, multi-consumer FIFO with push/<< to enqueue and pop (deq/shift) to block until an item arrives, and Thread::SizedQueue adds a bound so push blocks once the limit is reached. What replaces the classic structure is these classes plus a consumer thread - all locking semantics live inside the queue, and close (with closed?) terminates consumers deterministically instead of a nil sentinel. A plain Array remains idiomatic for a same-thread tick drain, where no synchronization is needed.
code_sketch:
require 'thread'

events = Thread::Queue.new
consumer = Thread.new { loop { handle(events.pop) } }   # pop blocks until an item arrives

events << Event.new(:sound, :bloop, 0.8)                # sender is never blocked

events.close                                            # consumers finish after draining
consumer.join
pitfalls: Array#shift and Array are not thread-safe: a shared array used as a queue loses or duplicates events under contention - use Thread::Queue.

After close, push/<< raises ClosedQueueError and popping an empty closed queue returns nil (deq(true) raises ThreadError), so loop { handle(q.pop) } calls the handler with nil unless the loop tests for it.
SizedQueue#push blocks when the queue is full, so a producer can deadlock against a consumer that posts back into the same bounded queue.
